text: This airliner just fell thirty-eight thousand feet in three and a half minutes, with its nose pointed up.
It was Air France 447, an Airbus A330 flying from Rio to Paris with two hundred twenty-eight people on board.
It was the middle of the night over the Atlantic, at thirty-five thousand feet, near a band of storms.
Then tiny ice crystals clogged the tubes that measure its speed.
The speed readings went haywire, and the autopilot shut off.
The pilot flying pulled the nose up. The jet climbed to thirty-eight thousand feet and kept losing speed.
Then a warning blared: stall. The wings could no longer hold the plane up.
Soon the ice melted, and the speed readings came back. But the nose stayed up.
Nose high, the plane sank belly first, almost eleven thousand feet a minute.
To get out of a stall, you lower the nose. In the dark, with alarms going off, the crew never got it back.
Three and a half minutes after it started falling, it hit the ocean. All two hundred twenty-eight people died.
Its black boxes sat about thirteen thousand feet underwater for nearly two years.
After the crash, that speed tube model was banned on Airbus jets.
Today pilots train for this exact moment: when the speed readings fail, hold a steady nose and steady power.
Two days ago, a jet over Florida also reported ice before it fell. Its cause is still unknown. Subscribe to see what investigators find.
